chapters.title: Chapter 7: Portfolio Integration and Risk Management

lessons.title: Sizing Positions Driven by Alternative Data Signals

body.text: A validated signal tells you which way to lean. It does not, by itself, tell you how hard to lean, and getting that second question wrong can undo all the careful work in the previous six chapters.

children.text: Every chapter so far has built toward a trustworthy, cost-aware signal. This chapter turns that signal into an actual portfolio: how much to size each position, how signals interact with each other and with crowding across the market, and what to do when a signal that used to work stops working. This lesson starts with sizing.
From Z-Score to Position Weight: The Basic Building Block

The simplest sizing rule scales a position linearly with the strength of the cross-sectional z-score from Chapter 4, subject to a hard cap so no single signal reading, however extreme, can push one position to an unreasonable share of the portfolio.

body.caption: BaseWeight is the portfolio weight assigned per one unit of z-score, MaxWeight is the desk's hard position cap, and z_i is the stock's current signal z-score.

body.title: Calculate a Signal-Scaled Position Weight
body.prompt: Your desk uses a BaseWeight of 0.5% per unit of z-score and a MaxWeight cap of 2%. A stock currently has a signal z-score of 2.5. What position weight, as a percentage, should it receive?
body.explanation: Raw scaled weight = 0.5% x 2.5 = 1.25%, which is below the 2% cap, so the position weight is 1.25%. If the z-score had instead been 5, the raw scaled weight of 2.5% would have been capped down to 2%, exactly what the cap is there to prevent.

children.text: Confidence-Weighted Sizing: Why the Same Z-Score Shouldn't Always Get the Same Size

The basic formula treats every z-score of 2.0 identically, regardless of which signal produced it. That is a mistake once you have Chapter 5's ICIR in hand: a signal with a long, consistent track record deserves more conviction at a given z-score than a newer, noisier one, even if both happen to be flashing the same reading today.

body.title: Same Z-Score, Different Track Record
body.scenario: Two signals are both currently showing a z-score of 2.0 on the same stock. Signal A is the desk's established web-traffic signal, with an ICIR of 0.6 measured over three years. Signal B is a newly built satellite-based signal, tested for only eight months, with an ICIR of 0.2 so far.
body.prompt: Should these two z-scores of 2.0 translate into the same position size? What would you actually do differently, and why?
body.modelAnswer: No, they should not translate into the same size. Signal A's higher ICIR over a much longer track record means its historical readings have been more consistently informative, so a z-score of 2.0 from Signal A carries more real evidence behind it. Signal B's lower ICIR and much shorter history mean the same numerical z-score is a noisier, less proven read, closer to the kind of short-history uncertainty flagged in Chapter 6's overfitting lesson. In practice, this should show up as a confidence multiplier applied on top of the basic sizing formula, scaling Signal B's contribution down relative to Signal A's, even though the raw z-score inputs look identical today. As Signal B accumulates a longer, validated track record, its multiplier should be allowed to rise toward parity with Signal A's, not before.

children.text: Volatility-Adjusted Sizing: Don't Let the Riskiest Stock Dominate

markDefs.definition: Scaling a position's size inversely to the stock's own volatility, so that two positions contribute similar amounts of risk to the portfolio even if their raw signal-based weights are identical.

children.text: Chapter 6 flagged that alt data's strongest signals often sit on less liquid, more volatile mid-cap and small-cap names. Without adjustment, two stocks with the same signal-based weight can contribute very different amounts of actual risk to the portfolio, simply because one of them moves around far more than the other.

markDefs.definition: The standard technique, borrowed from risk parity practice, of scaling each position's raw weight by the ratio of a target volatility level to the stock's own volatility, reducing the size of unusually volatile positions.

body.caption: A stock more volatile than the target gets scaled down, a stock less volatile than the target gets scaled up, up to any separate maximum weight cap still in force.

body.title: Apply Inverse-Volatility Scaling
body.prompt: Two stocks each have a raw signal-based weight of 1.5%. Stock A has an annualized volatility of 25%, matching the portfolio's target volatility of 25%. Stock B has an annualized volatility of 50%. What is Stock B's volatility-adjusted weight, as a percentage?
body.explanation: Stock A's adjusted weight stays at 1.5% x (25/25) = 1.5%, unchanged since its volatility already matches the target. Stock B's adjusted weight is 1.5% x (25/50) = 0.75%, cut in half because it is twice as volatile as the target. Without this adjustment, Stock B would have contributed roughly twice as much risk to the portfolio as Stock A, despite an identical raw signal-based weight.

children.text: Position Caps: Where Signal Sizing Meets Capacity

The MaxWeight cap in this lesson's basic formula should never be a single, static number chosen for the whole portfolio. It needs to be the smaller of two separate limits: a risk policy cap, reflecting how much of the portfolio your desk is willing to risk on any one idea, and the liquidity-based capacity limit from Chapter 6, reflecting what the stock's actual trading volume can support without excessive market impact. A signal can be strong enough to justify a 3% position by risk policy alone, while the stock's own liquidity genuinely supports only 1.5% at your fund's current AUM, and in that case the lower number always wins.

body.text: Position sizing is where every earlier chapter's discipline either pays off or gets thrown away. A perfectly validated signal, sized without regard to confidence, volatility, or liquidity, can still produce a portfolio that behaves nothing like the careful, decay-aware, cost-aware research that went into finding it.

The figures, formulas, and scenarios in this lesson are illustrative teaching examples for a general audience, not a complete risk management framework or a recommendation to trade any security. Position sizing for real capital should be built and reviewed with a qualified risk management function.

points: A basic sizing rule scales position weight linearly with a signal's z-score, subject to a hard cap: PositionWeight = min(MaxWeight, BaseWeight x z-score)

The same z-score from two different signals should not automatically get the same position size, a signal with a longer, higher-ICIR track record deserves more conviction than a newer, noisier one showing an identical reading

Inverse-volatility weighting scales a raw signal-based weight by the ratio of a target volatility to the stock's own volatility, preventing a single volatile position from dominating the portfolio's actual risk
Alt data's tendency to favour less liquid, more volatile names makes volatility adjustment especially important, not optional, for strategies built on it

A position's maximum weight should be the smaller of a risk policy cap and the liquidity-based capacity limit from Chapter 6, never a single static number chosen without reference to what the stock can actually absorb
Sizing is the step where every earlier discipline in this course, signal validation, decay awareness, cost realism, either gets carried through into the portfolio or quietly discarded
